The [preceding page](continuous-random-variables.qmd) explained why a continuous distribution assigns zero probability to an exact value. A table of point masses thus cannot describe how probability is arranged across the modeled duration support. If individual points have zero probability, what quantity lets us recover the probability of an interval?

We define density through interval area, verify the nonnegativity and unit-area requirements, and then interpret density height in relation to the measurement scale rather than as a point probability.

A [**probability density function**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html), abbreviated [**PDF**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html), describes how quickly probability accumulates near each value. It is a function $f_D:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying

$$
\mathbb{P}(D\in A)=\int_A f_D(d)\,\mathrm dd
$$

for every measurable set $A$. Probability is obtained by integration, not by reading the density at one point.

We estimate a descriptive density for the [Hillenbrand adult-men /i/ durations introduced on the preceding page](continuous-random-variables.qmd#hillenbrand-vowel-duration). Smoothing the observed values lets us compare a density height with the probability obtained by integrating over a duration interval. The bandwidth controls that smoothness and remains an analytical choice. Hillenbrand et al. did not fit or report this curve in the original study.

```{r}
#| label: load-hillenbrand-density
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
adult_i <- subset(vowels, speaker_type == "man" & vowel == "i")

stopifnot(
  nrow(vowels) == 1668L,
  nrow(adult_i) == 45L,
  !anyDuplicated(adult_i$speaker_id),
  !anyNA(adult_i$duration_ms)
)

density_fit <- density(
  adult_i$duration_ms,
  from = min(adult_i$duration_ms) - 6 * bw.nrd0(adult_i$duration_ms),
  to = max(adult_i$duration_ms) + 6 * bw.nrd0(adult_i$duration_ms),
  n = 4096
)
density_curve <- data.frame(
  duration_ms = density_fit$x,
  density_per_ms = density_fit$y
)
density_function <- approxfun(
  density_curve$duration_ms,
  density_curve$density_per_ms,
  yleft = 0,
  yright = 0
)
```

This page uses a Gaussian kernel density estimate (KDE) as a descriptive
smoother. Each observed duration contributes a small normal-shaped kernel;
their average forms the curve. R's `bw.nrd0()` chooses the default bandwidth,
which controls the smoothness, and `density()` evaluates the curve on 4,096
grid points. Extending the grid six bandwidths beyond the observed extrema
makes omitted tail area negligible for the numerical check. `approxfun()` then
linearly interpolates between grid points so `integrate()` can evaluate areas.
These settings define the numerical smoother used below. They were not part of
the Hillenbrand design, and a different bandwidth would produce a different
descriptive shape.

## Area, not height

The distinction between density and probability is visible in

$$
\mathbb{P}(D=d)=0
$$

even when $f_D(d)>0$. The height describes how quickly probability accumulates near $d$; it is not the probability of exactly $d$.

We use the observed median as the center of a one-millisecond recording bin and integrate the fitted density over that bin.

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-density-area
median_duration <- unname(quantile(adult_i$duration_ms, 0.5, type = 1))
bin_lower <- median_duration - 0.5 # dqr-allow: scale-boundary
bin_upper <- median_duration + 0.5 # dqr-allow: scale-boundary
bin_probability <- integrate(
  density_function,
  lower = bin_lower,
  upper = bin_upper,
  subdivisions = 1000L
)$value

grid_width <- diff(density_curve$duration_ms[1:2])
total_area <- sum(
  head(density_curve$density_per_ms, -1) +
    tail(density_curve$density_per_ms, -1)
) * grid_width / 2

stopifnot(
  bin_probability > 0,
  bin_probability < 1,
  abs(total_area - 1) < 0.002
)

c(lower_ms = bin_lower,
  upper_ms = bin_upper,
  fitted_interval_probability = bin_probability,
  fitted_total_area = total_area)
```

Thus the fitted interval probability is

$$
\mathbb{P}(d-.5<D<d+.5)
=\int_{d-.5}^{d+.5}f_D(u)\,\mathrm du,
$$

where the displayed code sets $d$ to the observed median. The resulting probability is `r sprintf("%.4f", bin_probability)`. It is area over a one-millisecond bin, not the density height at the median.

Three quantities should not be conflated. `density_function(d)` is a fitted
height in units of probability per millisecond. `bin_probability` is the KDE
area over a one-millisecond interval. `mean(adult_i$duration_ms == d)` is the
empirical proportion stored at the exact integer $d$. Only the last uses
unsmoothed row counts, and only the middle is an interval probability under the
KDE.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-density
#| fig-cap: "Raw adult-men /i/ durations and a kernel density estimate. The rug shows every observed token."
ggplot(adult_i, aes(duration_ms)) +
  geom_density(fill = "lightgrey", color = "steelblue") +
  geom_rug(color = "grey") +
  labs(x = "Vowel duration (ms)", y = "Density (per ms)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Checking the PDF requirements

A density must be nonnegative:

$$
f_D(d)\geq0
\qquad\text{for every }d.
$$

Its total area must equal one:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_D(d)\,\mathrm dd=1.
$$

These conditions concern area, so a density height may exceed one when probability is concentrated on a narrow interval. That fact does not produce a probability larger than one.

## Interpreting density in measurement units

The density $f_D(d)$ has units reciprocal to those of $D$. Because $D$ is measured in milliseconds, $f_D(d)$ is measured per millisecond. Multiplying by an interval width in milliseconds cancels the units and produces a unitless probability.

This unit check is another reason not to interpret density height as probability. The two objects have different units as well as different mathematical roles.

## Check your understanding

1. Modify `bin_lower` and `bin_upper` to span five milliseconds around the empirical median. How does the fitted interval probability change?
2. Why can a density height exceed one without producing a probability larger than one?
3. What does `density_function(median_duration)` describe, and what does it not describe?
4. Which parts of this page come from the observed Hillenbrand tokens, and which part is the descriptive smoothing model?
5. If the KDE bandwidth is doubled, has the observed dataset changed? What has
   changed?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Expanding the interval to 237.5–242.5 ms raises the fitted KDE probability from 0.009857 for the one-millisecond interval to 0.049246 for the five-millisecond interval. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Density has inverse-measurement units, so its height may exceed one while probability remains the area under the curve and the total area remains one. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. `density_function(240)` is the fitted density height, about 0.009857 per millisecond; it is neither a point probability nor an interval probability. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The 45 duration tokens and their histogram are observed Hillenbrand data, whereas `density()` supplies the descriptive kernel-smoothing model. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The rows do not change. The smoother changes how their empirical mass is
   spread across nearby modeled durations, so heights and interval areas may
   change.

</details>

Density is height per measurement unit, whereas probability is area over an
interval. A KDE estimates that descriptive density, with a shape that depends
on the smoothing choices. The [next
page](cumulative-distribution-functions.qmd) gives one threshold function that
applies to both discrete and continuous distributions.
